Interactive operating guide

Run your rig, end to end

pyBehaviorLab drives fully-automated mazes and operant chambers from one interface, with deep-learning behavioural tracking that can drive the task on a pyControl microcontroller. Set the six switches above to your rig, the whole guide adapts its screenshots, terminology, instructions, code skeletons and the ready-to-paste AI authoring prompt to match. Running a poke-only chamber with no camera? Set Camera → None and the tracking steps drop out.

You are configuring: Operant One camera per box Blob tracker No audio No mic 5-CSRTT
Orientation

The main window

Operant mode (python pyOperant.py) packs every chamber into one compact row inside a multi-tab window, so a wall of boxes fits on one screen.

Maze mode (python pyMaze.py) gives each arena its own tab with a large live-camera view, the right shape when position in space is the experiment.

The workflow, once Both modes follow the same five steps: create the experiment and cohort, connect the boards, configure the cameras, configure tracking and position triggers, then run and monitor.You've chosen a headless rig, no camera, no tracking. That drops steps 3 and 4 entirely: create the experiment and cohort, connect the boards, then run and monitor. Everything the animal does is sensed by the board itself (beam breaks, licks, levers), which is the classic operant configuration. Everything you set is saved with the project and restored on the next load.

The hardware under the software

Each setup is one microcontroller board plus its peripherals. The breakout board is the hub: every poke wall, lickometer, door motor, audio board and sensor plugs into it, and the pin map you write in the hardware definition (step 6) mirrors exactly what you see here.

Port numbering, check before you wire The silkscreen labels ten jacks PORT-1…PORT-10, but the software class Breakout_F767_v2 defines nine; it has port_1, port_2 and port_4…port_10, with no port_3. Breakout_F767_v1 does define all ten. If a device is plugged into the jack silkscreened PORT-3, confirm which board class your hardware definition instantiates, or that device simply cannot be addressed. Only port_4 and port_8 carry DAC + I²C (needed by the DAC audio board); port_1 and port_7 are the pair a Five_poke wall spans.
Step 1

Create the experiment & enter the cohort

A project holds the invariants of your rig, setups, cameras, ROIs, zones, tracking. Subjects and tasks are chosen per run. Start from an empty window and add one setup per physical box.

  1. Add one setup per apparatus with Add Box / Remove Box.
  2. Open Experimental info 8 and enter the experimenter and project name. These are written into the header of every data file, so sessions stay attributable.
  3. Set the data directory only if you need to, sessions are written beneath it by task and date, so runs never overwrite one another.
  4. Leave Track HD / task snapshots on (recommended). Each task and hardware-definition file is stored with the project under a content hash, and the same hash lands in the session header, an exact record of what ran, even if you edit the source later.
  5. Enter animals with Load Metadata (import an Excel cohort) or Edit Metadata. The first two columns, Subject and SetupID, are required: picking a subject in the GUI then binds the correct setup automatically. Extra columns (cage, ear-tag, group, sex…) ride along into the records.
  6. Press Save 6 once; after that, changes autosave. Load restores everything, setups, cameras, regions, zones and tracking.
Per-box, always Every board and camera operation is strictly per setup. A box you leave un-ticked is never touched, so you can re-flash or restart one setup while the others keep running.
Step 2

Connect & configure the pyControl boards

Each setup is driven by its own pyControl microcontroller running MicroPython. Once a task is uploaded it executes on the board in real time, independent of the PC. Four dialogs off the Setup Control row 19 manage the boards; each lists the setups with a tick-box so an action hits only the boards you choose.

Keep the flash drive off Disable Flash Drive (use the virtual COM port) during experiments, a mounted USB drive on the board interferes with serial communication. DFU Mode is only for updating MicroPython itself.
Step 3

Configure the cameras

Cameras, not needed for this rig

You've selected no camera. Skip this step and the next one entirely, leave Camera Config and Tracking Config untouched, and the pipeline never starts a camera, a tracker or a video writer.

What a headless rig still records Everything the board senses: the MCU .tsv with every state, event and print on the firmware clock, plus the task/hardware content hashes. There is simply no .mp4 or _video_data.txt, because there is no video. Live Status, Session Plot and Statistics all work normally; they read the MCU stream, not the camera.
Adding a camera later Nothing here is one-way. Plug a camera in, come back to Camera Config, assign it and draw a region, and the same project starts recording video alongside the MCU log, the boards and tasks you already set up are untouched.

Recording and tracking share one captured stream and one per-setup ROI, so the stored video is exactly what the tracker sees. Open Camera Config from Camera Control 7; the dialog has three tabs, worked left to right. It only needs doing at the start, or when the camera arrangement changes.

A · Setups & cameras

One camera per box, you're assigning a dedicated camera to each setup. Pick the camera for each setup from the ID list; Refresh camera IDs re-scans after you plug cameras in.

Shared camera (CCTV), one camera's image is split into a separate ROI per setup, so several boxes come off a single stream. Assign the shared camera, then you'll carve the ROIs on tab C.

Press Detect on each camera to measure the resolutions and frame rates it can truly deliver. The result is cached for this PC + camera, and the session data keeps the requested target rate distinct from the measured acquisition rate.

B · Camera options

Choose resolution and frame rate. For USB cameras the recommended MJPEG pixel format cuts USB bandwidth at higher resolutions versus uncompressed. Mirror / Flip fixes orientation per camera; Output quality sets recorded-video compression.

C · Regions, lens & connect

Press Draw regions and draw one rectangular ROI per setup on the live image. An ROI is required for both camera arrangements, it defines the region used for display, recording and tracking. Record selection chooses which setups write video. Optionally run Lens calibration with a printed checkerboard. Turn on Auto-connect cameras when this project loads if the rig is stable, then press Connect Cameras.

Under the hood, ROIs are resolution-independent Each ROI is stored as a normalized rectangle plus the resolution it was drawn at, and pixels are derived live from the current frame. Reopening the project, or restarting a camera at a different resolution, re-projects the ROI cleanly instead of drifting. If a saved ROI ever can't fit the live frame, the box says so rather than silently cropping the wrong region.
Step 4

Configure tracking, zones & triggers

Tracking, not used on this rig

No camera means no tracking: no zones, no c.* coordinates, no zone_changed events. Your task reacts purely to what the board senses, beam breaks in the poke wall, licks, lever presses, and to its own timers. Jump to step 5, or to step 6 for the task skeleton.

Reacting without a camera A rig with no camera still reacts, on hardware events instead of position: an IR beam break is delivered to the state machine in about a millisecond, which is faster and more reliable than any video route. Video tracking earns its place when the variable of interest is where the animal is, not what it touched.

Tracking turns live video into behavioural variables, for offline analysis and for driving the task as it runs. The animal's position or pose is resolved against named zones, optionally converted to metric units, and selected information is pushed to the microcontroller as events or task variables. Open Tracking Config from Camera Control 7; three tabs, left to right.

A · Zone Editor

  1. Pick the box in the selector 1, then a shape, Rectangle, Ellipse, Polygon, Manual Poly or Line, draw it on the live image and name it. For a T-maze, the classic set is LeftArm, RightArm, Stem.Typical operant zones: Home and Reward corners of the box. Zone names are the contract with the task, match its zone list exactly.
  2. Refine: drag to move, Ctrl+drag to rotate, drag the square handles to resize; Attach edges + the magnet snap neighbouring zones; Copy zones to all boxes replicates the layout.
  3. Draw the metric scale 4: type the real length + unit, press Draw Scale, drag over a feature of known size. This converts pixels to physical units, so distance and speed are stored in metric.
  4. Press Save Zones to Project 3, a zones-only commit, kept even if you later close the dialog with Discard. Export Box Zones 2 writes a snippet file for reuse on another rig; it does not save to the project.

B · Tracking Settings, choose your tracker

Select the backend. Your pick above is Blob tracker, its setup:

Blob uses background subtraction and needs no trained model. Capture an empty-arena reference with Retake BG, then tune the threshold and area. Click Auto Threshold to let the app estimate a good threshold from the current frame (Li's method) instead of hand-tuning a number.

no background needed Simple (self-norm) is background-free: each frame is divided by its own blur to cancel uneven lighting, then auto-thresholded (Li's method). There is no "capture background" step, and it shrugs off lighting drift and a stale reference. Best for a consistently dark (or light) animal against the arena; use background subtraction instead when animal and floor are close in brightness.

Where to click On Tracking Settings, click the Simple chip, second in the row, between Blob and DLC. Retake BG, the BG: dropdown and the fixed Threshold all grey out, because none of them mean anything without a background; Min/Max area still apply. Under the hood Simple is the Blob tracker with BG: set to self_norm, so the chip and the dropdown are two views of one setting and follow each other.

Open Calibrate… and press Auto Threshold: it estimates the contrast ratio from the live image and proposes a Min/Max area window from the animal it finds. Until you do, the ratio reads auto and is derived from the first frame. Its own row adds Lighting blur (0 = automatic, one twentieth of the frame height), Texture blur (10) and Speck size (10), mousefinder's own values, so it works out of the box on a textured floor. Each carries a detailed tooltip; hover before changing one. Every value here is saved with the project and restored on load.

One caveat worth knowing: the last two are absolute pixel widths, so they bite harder the smaller your frame is. At 1080p the default Speck size costs about a fifth of the measured blob area; at 640×480 over half; at 320×240 it can erode a small animal away completely. On low-resolution cameras drop both to 3–5. And because erosion shrinks the contour, press Auto Threshold after changing Speck size so the area bracket is re-derived from the eroded mask.

DLC (DeepLabCut) uses a trained pose model to track individual body parts. Browse to the exported model, choose the body parts, set the confidence threshold, and pick the zone part, the body part that decides zone occupancy (Center in the example). Press Initialize to load the model.

SLEAP uses a trained SLEAP pose model. Browse to the model directory (a top-down model also takes its paired centroid model), choose body parts and the zone part, set confidence, and press Initialize. On a Jetson you can export an ONNX/TensorRT engine for speed; the export is cached and reused.

Optionally enable Optical Flow + Kalman smoothing to steady noisy detections, and save annotated video to burn the overlay into a copy.

C · Event & Trigger, position back to the task

Coord Mapping rows map a body part to c.* task variables the board can read (e.g. c.loc_center, c.speed from Center). Push to MCU chooses whether zone-change events, c.* coordinates and/or an optional per-frame pose event are transmitted. The Event Triggers table adds behavioural rules: each combines a condition (in_zone, not_in_zone, speed, distance, angle…), the body part and zone(s), the MCU event name, an optional threshold and a minimum hold time. A rule fires on the edge, when its condition becomes true, not continuously. VID and PLOT control whether it shows in the overlay and live plots.

The contract that fails silently A trigger's event name must match an event the uploaded task expects, or the board can't act on it. If a name isn't in the task's events list, the app now names it plainly in the log (rather than a misleading "port may be down"). Conditions needing an orientation axis (angle, facing) can't run on Blob/Simple, which give only a body-centre.
What changed, the dialog is transactional Close with Apply & Close to commit the whole configuration, zones, scale, tracker, model, triggers, to the running pipeline and the project at once. Discard rolls the live preview back to how it was on open (including zones drawn this session); Cancel stays put. To keep finished zone work without applying tracker settings, press Save Zones to Project, a zones-only commit that survives a later Discard. Export Config / Export Box Zones write reusable snippet files only; Import stages one back into the dialog to commit with everything else. A box with zones must have a scale, and a pose box must have a model, or the commit tells you which is missing. Boxes currently recording are skipped by zone changes, their geometry is frozen until Stop.
Verify before you run Use Test Tracking from Camera Control 7 to walk the whole path, acquisition → tracking → zone detection → task events, before an animal is in the rig. It dispatches on the tracker you actually selected and runs only on boxes with a configured tracker, a background (or Simple/self-norm mode) for blob, an initialised model for DLC/SLEAP; drawn zones alone are not a tracker. If a box can't start (no model, missing file, load failure) it names the box and the reason instead of doing nothing.
Step 5

Run, monitor & stop a session

  1. In the setup row, pick the task and press Upload 13–14. The Live Status log reports the upload, then every state change and event with a timestamp.
  2. Press Record to start: video, tracking and MCU logging start together on one shared clock, so frames and behavioural events align later with no extra sync hardware. The timer runs while recording; with several setups, sessions start and stop independently per box.
  3. Drive the protocol from Experiment Control M5: Pause halts/resumes, Next/Prev switch protocol stage, Doors opens the manual door panel, and Controls reads/writes the running board's task variables.
  4. Use each row's Controls 16 for direct read/write of the running board's task variables mid-session.
  5. If the camera or apparatus shifted, correct a zone with the Adjust Zone toolbar M6, pick the zone, then nudge, rotate or scale. It takes effect immediately and persists with the project, but not while that maze is recording: the buttons grey out for the duration of a recording so the session's zone events keep one meaning. Adjust between sessions or during a live preview.
  6. Follow behaviour live with Session Plot (the event raster of all running boxes in one scrollable view) and Statistics (live per-task trial counters), both on the Setup Control row 19.
  7. Press Stop to finalize. Files land in the project's data directory, one folder per task and date.
Master buttons respect running boxes Global start/stop acts only on eligible boxes: a box already running is locked out of a master start while idle boxes stay available. Recording is lossless, every captured frame is written to the video or accounted in _drops.tsv. Tracking prioritises the freshest frame (skips are accounted too); only the on-screen display drops silently.
Step 6

Write the task & hardware definition

The behavioural protocol is two MicroPython files uploaded to the board: a hardware definition (the rig's pin map, which devices sit on which ports) and a task (the state machine). The complete API and every cross-file contract live in docs/AI_AUTHORING_GUIDE.md; this section shows the skeleton for your rig selection and gives you a ready-made AI prompt.

The hardware definition for this rig

An operant HD instantiates the breakout board, then the chamber devices. This is the pyOS-5 layout: a five-choice wall of IR beam-break holes with stimulus LEDs (it spans two ports, Five_poke asserts that the first has POW_C and the second DIO_C, which is why it is port_1 + port_7), one reward receptacle, a stepper-driven peristaltic pump, and a house light whose absence is the timeout punishment:

A maze HD instantiates the breakout board, then the arena devices, doors on motor channels with end-stop switches, plus any pokes or lick ports in the arms:

from devices import *
import pyControl.hardware as _h

board = Breakout_F767_v2()                # ports 1, 2, 4-10, no port_3

# Five-choice wall: 5 IR beams + 5 stimulus LEDs -> events poke_1..poke_5,
# and .LED on each hole. Spans two ports by design.
five_poke   = Five_poke(ports=[board.port_1, board.port_7])
# Reward receptacle, its own poke, conventionally poke_6.
reward_port = Poke(port=board.port_2, rising_event='poke_6',
                   falling_event='poke_6_out')
# Peristaltic pump on stepper channel M1: pump.forward(rate, n_steps).
pump        = Stepper_motor(direction_pin='PG9', step_pin='PG13')
enable_pump = _h.Digital_output(pin='PD9')
# House light on a spare POW line; off() = timeout.
houselight  = _h.Digital_output(pin=board.port_5.POW_A)
from devices import *
import pyControl.hardware as _h

board = Breakout_F767_v2()                # ports 1, 2, 4-10 (no port 3)
home_door  = Door(motor=board.motor1, limit_close_pin='PC5',
                  limit_open_pin='PD8')   # open()/close()/home()
left_door  = Door(motor=board.motor2, limit_close_pin='PB11')
reward_port = Poke(port=board.port_2, rising_event='poke_reward',
                   falling_event='poke_reward_out')

Your audio pick, DAC audio board. Needs a port carrying DAC + I²C (port_4 or port_8 on the V2 breakout). One line in the HD, classic API in the task:

speaker = Audio_board(port=board.port_8)   # task: hw.speaker.sine(5000),
                                           # .noise(), .clicks(10), .off(),
                                           # .set_volume(0-127)

The photometry connector uses both DAC pins, a box runs photometry LED control or an Audio_board, never both.

Your audio pick, I2S amplifier. Modern digital audio (TAS5825M with volume control, or the strap-pin PCM5102). Pre-render stimuli once, replay latency-free:

speaker = TAS5825MAudio()        # or PCM5102Audio(); pins per the guide
# task, in run_start():   hw.speaker.load_sweep(10000, 15000, ms=80, name='cue')
# task, in a state:       hw.speaker.play('cue')
#                         hw.speaker.play_sine(10000, 100, ramp_ms=5, level=0.5)

Keep stimuli below ~21.6 kHz (Nyquist at 48 kHz), and build ONE buffer at a time, a 300 ms stereo tone is ~115 KB and the MCU heap is small.

Your mic pick, ESP32-S3 sound sensor. A calibrated dB(A) meter on the dedicated ESP UART header:

mic = ESP_mic(uart=board.esp_uart1.UART, tx=board.esp_uart1.TX,
              rx=board.esp_uart1.RX)     # task: dBL, dBR = hw.mic.read_levels()

Poll read_levels() from a repeating timer state. Only alert_event/alert_off_event are real framework events, if you use them, both names must be in the task's events list.

The task skeleton, 5-CSRTT

The 5-choice serial reaction time task measures sustained attention and impulsivity. One of five holes lights for the stimulus duration; the animal must poke that hole to earn milk at the receptacle. Four outcomes are scored, and three of them cost a timeout:

OutcomeWhat the animal didConsequence
CorrectPoked the lit hole during the stimulus or the limited hold20 µl reward
IncorrectPoked a different hole5 s timeout (house light off)
PrematurePoked during the ITI, before any stimulus5 s timeout
OmissionDid not poke before the limited hold expired5 s timeout

Training runs in stages of increasing difficulty, the stimulus duration shortens (down to ~0.8 s) while the ITI lengthens (5 s at baseline). Because every outcome is print()ed with a stable name, the live Statistics tab computes accuracy, %omissions and %premature straight from the session.

from pyControl.utility import *
import hardware_definition as hw

states = ['inter_trial', 'stimulus', 'limited_hold',
          'reward_available', 'timeout']
events = ['poke_1', 'poke_2', 'poke_3', 'poke_4', 'poke_5',   # 5-choice wall
          'poke_6',                                            # reward receptacle
          'iti_timer', 'stim_timer', 'hold_timer',
          'timeout_timer', 'collect_timer', 'session_timer']
initial_state = 'inter_trial'

# Stage parameters, shorten SD / lengthen ITI as training advances.
v.stimulus_duration = 2 * second
v.iti_duration      = 5 * second
v.limited_hold      = 2 * second
v.timeout_duration  = 5 * second
v.session_duration  = 30 * minute
v.reward_steps      = 200          # pump steps per reward
v.step_rate         = 500
v.n_correct = 0
v.n_incorrect = 0
v.n_premature = 0
v.n_omission = 0
v.target = 0

HOLES = ('poke_1', 'poke_2', 'poke_3', 'poke_4', 'poke_5')

def _hole(n):
    return getattr(hw.five_poke, 'poke_{}'.format(n))

def run_start():
    # v.* defaults are re-applied on Upload, not on Record, re-seed here.
    v.n_correct = v.n_incorrect = v.n_premature = v.n_omission = 0
    hw.houselight.on()
    set_timer('session_timer', v.session_duration)

def run_end():
    hw.off()

def inter_trial(event):
    if event == 'entry':
        set_timer('iti_timer', v.iti_duration)
    elif event in HOLES:                      # poked before the stimulus
        v.n_premature += 1
        print('Premature_response')
        disarm_timer('iti_timer')             # set_timer survives transitions
        goto_state('timeout')
    elif event == 'iti_timer':
        goto_state('stimulus')

def stimulus(event):
    if event == 'entry':
        v.target = randint(1, 5)
        _hole(v.target).LED.on()
        print('Stimulus: {}'.format(v.target))
        set_timer('stim_timer', v.stimulus_duration)
    elif event == 'exit':
        _hole(v.target).LED.off()
    elif event == 'stim_timer':
        goto_state('limited_hold')
    elif event in HOLES:
        _score(event)

def limited_hold(event):                      # stimulus is off, clock still runs
    if event == 'entry':
        set_timer('hold_timer', v.limited_hold)
    elif event in HOLES:
        _score(event)
    elif event == 'hold_timer':
        v.n_omission += 1
        print('Omission')
        goto_state('timeout')

def _score(event):
    if int(event[-1]) == v.target:
        v.n_correct += 1
        print('Correct_response')
        goto_state('reward_available')
    else:
        v.n_incorrect += 1
        print('Incorrect_response')
        goto_state('timeout')

def reward_available(event):
    if event == 'entry':
        hw.pump.forward(v.step_rate, v.reward_steps)
        print('Reward_delivered')
        set_timer('collect_timer', 10 * second)
    elif event == 'poke_6':                   # collected at the receptacle
        print('Reward_collected')
        goto_state('inter_trial')
    elif event == 'collect_timer':
        goto_state('inter_trial')

def timeout(event):
    if event == 'entry':
        hw.houselight.off()                   # the punishment is darkness
        set_timer('timeout_timer', v.timeout_duration)
    elif event == 'exit':
        hw.houselight.on()
    elif event == 'timeout_timer':
        goto_state('inter_trial')

def all_states(event):
    if event == 'session_timer':
        stop_framework()
Why those print strings Correct_response / Incorrect_response / Omission / Premature_response are the names the live-stats configs count. Keep them stable and the Statistics tab gives you accuracy and %omissions with no extra work; rename them and the counters silently read zero.

Probabilistic reversal learning measures behavioural flexibility. The animal initiates each trial at the centre hole and then chooses left or right; one side pays off with high probability, the other with low. Once performance on the good side crosses a threshold, the contingency silently reverses after a random number of trials, and the animal has to notice and switch.

The key trick is a moving average of choices: it, not a fixed trial count, decides when a reversal is due, so a fast learner reverses sooner. Note the pattern below: a class instance like exp_mov_ave lives happily on v., but it is invisible to the GUI and to print_variables, so mirror the scalar you care about.

from pyControl.utility import *
import hardware_definition as hw

states = ['init_trial', 'choice_state', 'left_reward',
          'right_reward', 'inter_trial_interval']
events = ['poke_2', 'poke_3', 'poke_4', 'session_timer']   # 3 = centre
initial_state = 'init_trial'

v.session_duration = 1 * hour
v.ITI_duration     = 1 * second
v.threshold        = 0.70            # moving average that triggers a reversal
v.tau              = 8               # trials, time constant of that average
v.trials_post_threshold = [5, 15]    # random delay before the reversal lands
v.good_prob = 0.9
v.bad_prob  = 0.1
v.n_trials = 0
v.n_blocks = 0
v.good_side = choice(['left', 'right'])
v.correct_mov_ave = exp_mov_ave(tau=v.tau, init_value=0.5)
v.ave_correct = 0.5                  # scalar mirror, the GUI can't see the object
v.threshold_crossed = False
v.trials_till_reversal = 0

def run_start():
    v.n_trials = 0
    v.n_blocks = 0
    set_timer('session_timer', v.session_duration)

def init_trial(event):
    if event == 'entry':
        hw.five_poke.poke_3.LED.on()          # centre light = trial available
    elif event == 'exit':
        hw.five_poke.poke_3.LED.off()
    elif event == 'poke_3':
        goto_state('choice_state')

def choice_state(event):
    if event == 'entry':
        hw.five_poke.poke_2.LED.on()
        hw.five_poke.poke_4.LED.on()
    elif event == 'exit':
        hw.five_poke.poke_2.LED.off()
        hw.five_poke.poke_4.LED.off()
    elif event == 'poke_2':
        _outcome('left')
    elif event == 'poke_4':
        _outcome('right')

def _outcome(side):
    v.n_trials += 1
    if side == v.good_side:
        rewarded = withprob(v.good_prob)
        v.correct_mov_ave.update(1)
        print('Correct_response')
    else:
        rewarded = withprob(v.bad_prob)
        v.correct_mov_ave.update(0)
        print('Incorrect_response')
    v.ave_correct = v.correct_mov_ave.value          # keep the mirror fresh
    print('ave_correct: {}'.format(v.ave_correct))
    _maybe_reverse()
    timed_goto_state('left_reward' if side == 'left' else 'right_reward', 0) \
        if rewarded else timed_goto_state('inter_trial_interval', 0)

def _maybe_reverse():
    if v.threshold_crossed:
        v.trials_till_reversal -= 1
        if v.trials_till_reversal == 0:
            v.good_side = 'left' if v.good_side == 'right' else 'right'
            v.correct_mov_ave.value = 1 - v.correct_mov_ave.value
            v.threshold_crossed = False
            v.n_blocks += 1
            print('Reversal: good_side now {}'.format(v.good_side))
    elif v.correct_mov_ave.value > v.threshold:
        v.threshold_crossed = True
        v.trials_till_reversal = randint(*v.trials_post_threshold)
        print('threshold_crossed')

def all_states(event):
    if event == 'session_timer':
        stop_framework()
The full version ships with the app tasks/ReversalLearning/ReversalLearning_final.py is the complete, rig-tested implementation (pump volumes, reward states, per-block bookkeeping), the skeleton above is that task reduced to its logic so you can read it in one screen.

Spontaneous alternation in a T-maze measures working memory with no reward and no training: a mouse that remembers where it just went prefers the other arm. One forced sample trial, then free choices, and the whole protocol is driven by where the animal is, which is why this one needs the camera and tracker you configured in steps 3–4.

Two idioms make a position-driven task robust, and both appear below. POLL re-checks position on entry and on every tracker update, because the animal may already be in the zone when the state begins. The one-shot latch means a centroid flickering on a zone boundary can't score the same trial twice.

from pyControl.utility import *
import hardware_definition as hw

states = ['init_state', 'habituation', 'open_sample_arm', 'sample_arm',
          'return_to_center', 'choice_phase', 'last_state']
# zone_changed / frame_event are host-fired intrinsic events (auto-registered,
# silent, they write no .tsv row).
events = ['zone_changed', 'frame_event', 'end_task_timer']
initial_state = 'init_state'

v.start_arm = 'R'                  # forced-sample side; never written by the task
v.last_arm  = 'R'                  # arm most recently visited, alternation is scored vs this
v.n_correct = 0
v.n_incorrect = 0
v.trial_num = 0
v.max_trial_number = 14
v.session_limit = 15 * minute
v.choice_made = False              # one-shot latch, reset on entry

c.loc_center = 0                   # zone name of the tracked part ("" = no zone)

# These names must match the Zone Editor exactly.
left_zones   = ['LeftArm']
right_zones  = ['RightArm']
center_zones = ['Center_MidZone']

POLL = ('entry', 'zone_changed', 'frame_event')

def run_start():
    hw.HomeDoor_enable.on()        # enables are inverted: on() = driver energised
    hw.LeftDoor_enable.on()
    hw.RightDoor_enable.on()
    v.last_arm = v.start_arm
    v.n_correct = 0
    v.n_incorrect = 0
    v.trial_num = 0
    set_timer('end_task_timer', v.session_limit)

def run_end():
    hw.off()                       # run_end is AFTER teardown, only turn things off

def init_state(event):
    if event == 'entry':
        hw.home_door.close()       # known state before anything moves
        hw.left_door.close()
        hw.right_door.close()
        timed_goto_state('habituation', 5 * second)   # never goto_state() in entry

def choice_phase(event):
    if event == 'entry':
        hw.left_door.open()
        hw.right_door.open()
        v.choice_made = False      # latch reset
    if event not in POLL or v.choice_made:
        return                     # only position-relevant events do work
    chosen = None
    if   c.loc_center in left_zones:  chosen = 'L'
    elif c.loc_center in right_zones: chosen = 'R'
    if chosen:
        v.choice_made = True       # score this trial exactly once
        v.trial_num += 1
        if chosen != v.last_arm:
            v.n_correct += 1
            print('Correct_response')      # alternated
        else:
            v.n_incorrect += 1
            print('Incorrect_response')    # repeated the same arm
        v.last_arm = chosen
        timed_goto_state('return_to_center', 0)

def all_states(event):
    if event == 'end_task_timer':
        stop_framework()
The full version ships with the app tasks/TM_spontAlternation/SpontMaze_RightStart_v2.py is the complete protocol, habituation, forced sample, door sequencing and the return-to-centre states. The skeleton above keeps the scoring logic and the two idioms.

A minimal skeleton to start from. Tracking is configured on this rig, so the position hooks are included.This rig has no camera, so the task reacts to board events and timers only.

from pyControl.utility import *
import hardware_definition as hw

states = ['wait_for_poke', 'reward', 'inter_trial']
events = ['poke_1', 'poke_6', 'iti_timer', 'session_timer']
initial_state = 'wait_for_poke'

v.session_duration = 30 * minute
v.iti_duration = 2 * second
v.n_trials = 0

def run_start():
    v.n_trials = 0                       # v.* resets on Upload, not on Record
    set_timer('session_timer', v.session_duration)

def wait_for_poke(event):
    if event == 'entry':
        hw.five_poke.poke_1.LED.on()
    elif event == 'exit':
        hw.five_poke.poke_1.LED.off()
    elif event == 'poke_1':
        v.n_trials += 1
        print('Correct_response')
        goto_state('reward')

def reward(event):
    if event == 'entry':
        hw.pump.forward(500, 200)
        timed_goto_state('inter_trial', 1 * second)

def inter_trial(event):
    if event == 'entry':
        timed_goto_state('wait_for_poke', v.iti_duration)

def all_states(event):
    if event == 'session_timer':
        stop_framework()
from pyControl.utility import *
import hardware_definition as hw

states = ['wait_in_zone', 'reward', 'inter_trial']
events = ['zone_changed', 'frame_event', 'iti_timer', 'session_timer']
initial_state = 'wait_in_zone'

v.session_duration = 30 * minute
v.n_trials = 0
v.scored = False

c.loc_center = 0                         # zone name pushed by the tracker
target_zones = ['Reward']                # must match the Zone Editor

POLL = ('entry', 'zone_changed', 'frame_event')

def run_start():
    v.n_trials = 0
    set_timer('session_timer', v.session_duration)

def wait_in_zone(event):
    if event == 'entry':
        v.scored = False                 # one-shot latch
    if event not in POLL or v.scored:
        return
    if c.loc_center in target_zones:
        v.scored = True
        v.n_trials += 1
        print('Correct_response')
        timed_goto_state('reward', 0)

def reward(event):
    if event == 'entry':
        timed_goto_state('inter_trial', 1 * second)

def inter_trial(event):
    if event == 'entry':
        timed_goto_state('wait_in_zone', 2 * second)

def all_states(event):
    if event == 'session_timer':
        stop_framework()
The three contracts that fail silently 1. Every event the HD (or a tracking trigger) fires must appear verbatim in the task's events list. 2. Zone names in the task must match the Zone Editor exactly. 3. Module-level v.* defaults are re-applied on every Upload, re-seed per-run counters in run_start().

Let an AI write it, the prompt for this rig

The prompt below is rebuilt live from the five switches at the top, mode, camera, tracker, audio and mic. Copy it, paste it to your AI assistant together with the repository (or at least docs/AI_AUTHORING_GUIDE.md), and replace the last line with your protocol.

AI authoring prompt Operant Blob tracker 

      

      
Where the full reference lives
      docs/AI_AUTHORING_GUIDE.md documents the complete task API (timers, randomisation, staging, variables), every device class with its constructor signature, the ten-timer budget, and the upload pipeline. docs/AI_AUTHORING_PROMPT.md is the long-form companion prompt. Snapshots of whatever you upload are stored under <project>/source/ with content hashes, so every session records exactly which task and HD ran.

    


    
    

      
Reference

      
What a session writes

      
Every run finalizes into <data>/<project>/<task>/<date>/:

      

        
FileWhat it is

        
*.tsvThe MCU event log, every state and event on the firmware clock. Its header carries the djb2 content hashes of the exact task and hardware definition that ran.

        
*.mp4The session video, ROI-cropped to the setup, on the shared clock.

        
*_video_data.txtPer-frame tracking + synchronization: timestamps, firmware-clock anchor, and the tracked coordinates/pose.

        
*_drops.tsvFrame-drop accounting, always on, so any display or encoder skip is auditable.

      

    


    

      
Rules that bite

      

        !
Trigger event names must exist in the task. A tracking trigger named enter_A only works if the uploaded task lists enter_A in its events. A mismatch is now reported by name in the log.

        !
Blob & Simple give only a body-centre. Orientation conditions (head angle, facing) need a pose backend (DLC/SLEAP).

        !
Scale before zones ship. A box with zones must have a metric scale line, or Apply & Close tells you which box is missing it.

        !
Disable the board's flash drive during experiments; a mounted drive disturbs serial communication.

        !
Everything is per-box. Un-ticked setups are never touched, maintain one while the rest keep running.

        !
Zones freeze while recording. The adjust buttons grey out and the dialog skips recording boxes, a session's zone events must keep one meaning from Record to Stop.

        !
Export ≠ Save. The dialog's Export buttons write snippet files for reuse; only Apply & Close (everything) or Save Zones to Project (zones only) persist to the project.

        !
Zones alone are not a tracker. Test Tracking needs a configured backend, a blob background (or Simple mode) or an initialised pose model.
